The hydrogen tank and its associated manual valve account for over 40% of the identified scenarios, suggesting the importance of proper defueling and isolation procedures. Furthermore, pressure relief systems highlight that the safety of the facility relies on the ability to safely vent hydrogen during overpressure or thermal events. The remaining components’ diversity (e.g. fuel cell, shutoff valve, defueling valve, etc.) suggests that hazards may be present wherever there is pressurized hydrogen. Notably, many of the hazardous scenarios presented had featured the guideword “as well as” (see Appendix A for the complete list of unique HAZOP scenarios). This is because to create a hazardous scenario, other failsafes needed to be absent or non-functioning, or two components or mistakes had to occur simultaneously. The likelihood of these failures occurring together is lower than for isolated incidents, and this low likelihood is one of the reasons there were very few scenarios of high frequency (rating of “5”). It is important to emphasize that this is a qualitative analysis, not a definitive statement on relative risks for all possible systems. Risk levels categorized as “medium” or “high” risk in this assessment could be changed through more specific quantitative analysis, additional physical understanding of specific outcomes, or changes to a design that would make some outcomes less likely. Notably, the purpose of the risk levels presented in this work is to help identify and prioritize conditions that may require additional investigation into their likelihood and consequence. Additionally, these identified 26 higher-risk scenarios can form the basis for identifying and developing useful preventative and mitigative measures, some of which are discussed in the next section. 27 3. PREVENTATIVE AND MITIGATIVE MEASURES The numerous potential hazards identified and outlined in this report serve as a means of developing effective preventative and mitigative measures to enable safety of workers and property in a hydrogen rail maintenance facility. Indeed, the results from this study have helped highlight many design and procedural practices which should be considered when building or retrofitting a facility. Many of these suggested practices are similar to or reflective of the preventative measures provided by many in the literature as outlined in Section 0 of this report [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14]. 1.
